weeks.title: Claude Design sync and Vercel Eve advance verifiable agent workflows
weeks.summary: This week paired new agent surfaces—Claude Design sync, live Artifacts, Managed Agents, enterprise MCP auth, and Vercel's filesystem-first Eve framework—with a serious push toward verifiable autonomous coding loops. Open-weight experimentation was equally prominent: GLM 5.2 reportedly beat Opus 4.8 on Vercel's Next.js evals, while DwarfStar work emphasized preserving inference quality even when enormous DeepSeek models must stream from SSD.
details: Claude Code and Claude Design gained bidirectional /design-sync: teams can pull their actual design system into a repository and build with real components, then push implementations back to the canvas. Artifacts let Claude turn ongoing work into a shared live-updating page; examples included system diagrams, visual code explanations, animation previews, analyses, and dashboards. Managed Agents guidance focused on production problems such as credentials, sandboxing, and observability, while an Enterprise-Managed Auth MCP extension lets admins authorize connectors centrally so tools are ready at first login and access remains consistent across chat, Code, and Cowork.

Vercel described Eve as 'Next.js for agents': an agent is a filesystem directory whose minimal entry point is agent/instructions.md, with predictable tool files such as tools/query-db.ts and deployment producing Sandbox, Gateway, and Workflow infrastructure. The broader claim was that model competition makes a model-neutral AI SDK more valuable; GLM 5.2, an open model, had surpassed Opus 4.8 in Vercel's Next.js evals. V0 also committed to shipping strong default skills while accepting public or private team skills.

The recommended autonomous workflow was Claude Code plus a strong model and verifier in a loop, feeding it tasks—or the data needed to generate tasks—and removing bottlenecks. Agents were said to encourage open APIs, skills documentation, evals, CLIs, and machine-friendly Markdown/JSON/HTML. One concrete implementation used a GitHub Action to launch Codex, compare an issue against VISION.MD, and implement it only if it fit; worktreeinclude can control which files Codex copies into new worktrees.

Local inference posts prioritized capability over headline speed. Antirez ran the 433GB DeepSeek v4 PRO through DwarfStar on an M5 Max with 128GB using SSD streaming at 4.15 tokens/second and found that sufficient for a difficult security answer. His target configurations included a 512GB M3 Ultra or four distributed 128GB machines with 3-bit variants if quality holds, using Unsloth 4-bit weights initially and later optimizing quantization. He argued that DeepSeek's native formats may give it a local speed edge, but comparisons with 2–3-bit GLM 5.2 still require experiments.

Operationally, Codex advertised remote/local handoff and compatibility of its app, CLI, and SDK with open-source models, but also suffered capacity errors and promised rate-limit resets after fixes. Pi shipped security updates for undici, Mistral prompt caching, and smaller package imports. Shopify announced Claude, ChatGPT, and Perplexity connectors plus an AI Toolkit for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, recommending v0, Manus, Replit, or Lovable as routes to create a store if a merchant did not yet have one.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.
The emphasis was on real-world evaluation, executable evidence, and deterministic guardrails.

weeks.title: Claude Fable 5 launch erupts over Anthropic’s hidden model fallbacks
weeks.summary: Claude Fable 5 was presented as a step change from coding assistant to design and thought partner, but its undisclosed fallback safeguards triggered a sharp trust dispute and forced Anthropic to make model downgrades visible. Across Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and local inference, the dominant practical lesson was to build long-running, end-to-end-verifiable loops with isolated context, explicit success criteria, and security boundaries rather than continually steering individual prompts.
details: Anthropic staff said Fable 5 brought better judgment, taste, tool use, code quality, token efficiency, and self-verification, with one debugging example where it measured behavior, added logs, and verified the fix without harness prompting. Fable always thinks and can respond more slowly; high effort was recommended by default, with xhigh reserved for the hardest problems because even low or medium reportedly beat earlier models at xhigh in Anthropic's evals. Users can select claude-fable-5 in Claude Code/Cowork or use that model ID in the Messages API and Managed Agents.

The launch was marred by invisible safeguards for frontier-LLM development that silently fell back to Opus 4.8. Anthropic admitted that shipping quickly with narrowly targeted invisible controls was the wrong tradeoff and promised visible fallbacks plus API refusal reasons, while warning robust public classifiers would temporarily create more false positives. Dwarkesh called undisclosed sandbagging hostile and untrustworthy, even if the motivation was to prevent leakage of research capabilities learned from Anthropic's proprietary workflows; a reported security-review block was confirmed as a cyber-classifier false positive.

The strongest workflow advice was to give agents executable success criteria and let them run until verified. Suggested ingredients were auto permissions, dynamic workflows coordinating hundreds or thousands of agents, /goal or /loop persistence, cloud execution so the laptop can close, and browser or simulator tools for end-to-end checks. Steipete described an orchestrator waking every five minutes to direct repository threads, combining triage, autoreview, and computer-use skills; Codex ran for four days in multiple crabbox worktrees, tested an end-to-end-verifiable product, and even registered for needed services, leaving the human to enter payment details and reject misaligned work.

Context isolation became more explicit: Claude Code added nested subagents capped at depth five, and a proposed skill frontmatter option fork:true would give a skill its own context before it delegates isolated steps. Poteto advised beginning with no plugins, skills, or AGENTS.md, observing recurring failures, then encoding only those into custom skills—or better, lint rules and repository structures that make mistakes impossible. For Pi, a new trust prompt now appears before loading AGENTS.md or .pi from a folder, and users were reminded that a 4,000-token AGENTS.md itself has a context cost.

Open and local models were framed as both a capability hedge and a freedom hedge. DwarfStar's 2-bit DS4F was described as useful rather than frontier-grade and immune to provider restrictions, while antirez argued rapidly changing lab leadership reflects iterative RL, attention, and scaling improvements rather than permanent conceptual monopolies. He saw Chinese open weights as an escape from restricted frontier access; separately, his plan to centralize multi-machine agent logs and skills used Redis arrays with ARGREP.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
The emphasis was on real-world evaluation, executable evidence, and deterministic guardrails.
Teams focused on persistent loops, orchestration, parallel agents, and bounded autonomy.

We’re rolling out changes to make Fable 5’s safeguards for frontier LLM development visible.

Starting this week, flagged requests will visibly fall back to Opus 4.8—the same as our safeguards for cyber and bio. You will see this every time it happens. On the API, any flagged requests will return a reason for their refusal (coming to server-side fallback in the next few days).

We wanted to deploy Fable 5 to our users quickly and safely. Visible safeguards can be probed, so they have to be robust, which takes time to get right. Invisible safeguards can be targeted more narrowly, allowing us to ship quickly with very few false positives. We went with invisible safeguards for this reason—and that was the wrong tradeoff. You should have visibility into the safeguards we have in place, and why. We’re sorry for not getting the balance right.

Making the safeguards visible makes them easier to work around, so keeping them robust to jailbreaks will unfortunately mean more false positives while we improve the classifiers. We're also tuning our bio and cyber classifiers to trigger less often on harmless requests. We know this is frustrating and we’ll do our best to keep this period as short as possible.

If you think a request has been mistakenly flagged: run /feedback in Claude Code, click thumbs-down on the fallback in https://t.co/LtktniD5HY or Cowork, or file the safeguard appeal form for API requests. Your reports help us tune these classifiers and we appreciate your feedback.

sources.author: dwarkesh_sp
sources.text:
Re the Fable ML sandbagging, the model's AI research capabilities were probably at least partly trained on Anthropic employees diffing atop proprietary algos and infra.

So the IP leak is somewhat like a researcher who knows Anthropic's stack getting poached to another lab.

Anthropic's recent "When AI builds itself" post talks about a next-step eval. Where they snapshot a research session at the moment a human researcher made a suboptimal next-step choice, show a model only the transcript up to that point and ask what it would do next, then have a hindsight-equipped LLM judge decide whether the model's suggestion or the human's actual choice was better.

This eval seems like a very good RL target for AI R&D - one among many that could be used to have AIs emulate Anthropic researchers and their research products.

I'm just speculating. But if this was a motivation, then Anthropic should have figured out a better way to protect IP than sandbagging without telling the user they're sandbagging, which is very hostile and untrustworthy behavior.

weeks.title: Claude terminal API and Codex Python SDK enable durable agent loops
weeks.summary: Builders argued that the unit of work should shift from prompting one coding agent to designing loops that supervise agents, verify their output, and preserve enough execution state to recover. Product releases made that concrete through Claude's terminal API and background forks, Codex's Python SDK and business workflows, Vercel's persistent agent storage, and experiments with open models and local inference.
details: Claude Platform's ant CLI made every API endpoint terminal-accessible: it can call Messages, start a Managed Agent, send events, and retrieve a full trace of events, tool calls, and decisions when the run finishes or stalls. Claude Code can operate ant through the built-in /claude-api skill without glue code—for example listing sessions, uploading PDFs, or debugging runs. The revised /fork starts a background agent with the current system prompt, tools, history, model, and prompt cache and returns its result, while /branch retains the old behavior of copying a transcript into a user-driven session.

The workflow message was to encode manual checks so the model closes its own feedback loop and to design loops that prompt agents rather than repeatedly prompt agents by hand. One Codex user had OpenClaw supervise multiple Codex instances and configured an audible alert for human-only blockers such as npm releases protected by 1Password. Codex also became embeddable via the openai-codex Python SDK, while business users gained hosted/shared websites, broader plugins and skills, and visual annotations for feedback in documents, slides, and spreadsheets.

Infrastructure was adapting to long-running agents. Vercel decoupled filesystem state from Sandbox lifetime so it can be independently read, written, and attached to Builds, Functions, or Sandboxes, and argued that agent-native IDEs plus remote development fit large organizations where local environments are often unavailable. Pi's narrower durability design stores completed LLM responses, the portions of completed tool results sent back to the model, and the current phase—idle, streaming, tool execution, compaction, or retry—so a harness can resume, retry, or ask the user after a crash without pretending to solve full orchestration.

Local-model experimentation supplied concrete tradeoffs. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE designed for long-running agents, reportedly performed very well on Pi issues through OpenRouter. DwarfStar moved from requiring 128GB toward running on an ordinary good MacBook at lower speed; for V4 Flash 2-bit, antirez explained that 64GB can hold half the experts, biased MoE routing can yield roughly 70% cache hits, expert loading can overlap shared-expert computation, and layer streaming helps prefill. Misses remain costly: PRO ran around 4 tokens/second on an M5 Max versus 9–10 on an M3 Ultra, and 32GB changes the calculation substantially.

Reliability and evaluation claims were contested. Claude reset limits after an Opus 4.8 handling bug spawned too many parallel tool calls, prompting questions about its prerelease testing; Codex likewise reset paid-plan limits after three reliability incidents and disclosed a token-undercounting fix affecting under 15% of accounts. Antirez rejected DeepSWE's ordering beyond placing GPT-5.5 first and said a benchmark where Sonnet beats Opus should be debugged rather than published. On security, OpenClaw's mutable-display-name allowlist flaws were characterized as medium severity requiring adversarial same-workspace access and specific configuration, with ID-based configuration recommended over names.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.
The emphasis was on real-world evaluation, executable evidence, and deterministic guardrails.

sources.author: antirez
sources.text:
You are wrong on several levels :D But you are also partially right that it is slower.

1. V4 Flash 2bit is 80GB, if you have a 64GB machine, 50% of your experts are already in memory.
2. The hit rate is MUCH larger than 50%, because MoEs LLMs have a tedency to over use the same experts.
3. You can mask loading times a lot even during generation. As you do the inference of the shared expert, you already parallelize loading of the routed experts. And you can do this also for the routed experts that happen to be cache hits.
4. For prefill, streaming of whole layers works much better.

At the same time, misses are costly, so indeed the performance hit is real. But for instance right now I can run PRO at 4 t/s on my M5 Max, while it runs at 9/10 t/s on the M3 Ultra. This means that Flash could go at 15 t/s easily, I got 20 t/s in a few tests I did (focusing more on PRO) but I don't trust them as they were run on a 128 GB system. I'll write a tool to lock 64GB of memory in a total way using Metal, so that I can verify this result.

TLDR: it is slower but with the right tricks a lot can be done, and you can get 70% hits on a 64GB system. For a 32 GB system the math is a lot different.

sources.author: badlogicgames
sources.text:
definitely no step abstraction pi :)

durability is multi-layered. for pi's agent abstraction, durability is really just about:

- store completed LLM responses
- store completed tool execution results (only the parts that get send to the LLM, not the effects, e.g. file changes, separate concern)
- store phase we are in (idle, llm streaming, tools executing, compaction, retry)

if the agent goes belly up for some reason, that info is enough to let it pick up where it left. based on phase, harness can decide to auto-resume/retry, or let user give a choice.

that's the lowest possible level of durability. everything else, e.g. durable agent orchestration, can be built on top of that. i'm not trying to solve that tho.

weeks.title: Claude Opus 4.8 launches dynamic workflows amid benchmark credibility fights
weeks.summary: Coding agents were presented less as autocomplete than as long-running engineering systems: Claude Code added Opus 4.8, dynamic subagent workflows and reliability work, while Codex users described multi-hour goals, automated review, QA and migration tooling. The enthusiasm was tempered by arguments over benchmark credibility, token and permission costs, production complexity, privacy, and whether local inference products such as DwarfStar can deliver a better integrated experience.
details: Anthropic shipped Opus 4.8 in Claude Code, claiming stronger coding, greater honesty about uncertainty and self-detected bugs, similar default coding-token use to Opus 4.7 at high effort, and an xhigh setting for difficult asynchronous work. Its research-preview dynamic workflows write orchestration scripts and launch coordinated subagents for migrations, refactors, performance optimization, batch bug fixes and design stress tests; the advice was to use auto mode to avoid permission stalls, begin with a scoped task, and reserve the feature for large jobs because it consumes tokens quickly. Claude Code also added a security-guidance plugin, streamed thinking and tool calls, a full-screen renderer preview, visible and more robust compaction, recovery from oversized media, MCP fixes for connections, OAuth and proxy rate limits, and /claude-api migrate guidance. Opus 4.8 can accept authoritative system-role instructions mid-conversation without invalidating the existing prompt cache, and long-horizon work was explicitly paired with /goal or Managed Agents Outcomes.

Practitioners described concrete agent workflows rather than one-shot prompting. One Codex setup combined GPT 5.5, /goal, autoreview and crabbox to stretch tasks from roughly an hour to four-to-ten-hour runs; another generated a user test for every commit, exercised OpenClaw through webVNC plus Peekaboo/MCPorter computer and browser use, then opened fix PRs in the background. Codex was seen inventing an ad-hoc codemod for a large TypeScript migration, while pstack’s /poteto-mode turned an emergent StyleX refactoring behavior into a rule that agents should build codemods and custom skills for their own subagents. Workflow advice included telling a reviewer that a bug exists so it keeps searching, using autoreview to keep GPT honest, defining edge-case depth in AGENTS.md, and using Opus as a manager of other models in Cursor; Vercel likewise made its CLI a self-updating, dependency-free binary because agents increasingly onboard users through CLI, MCP and SDK interfaces.

Model comparisons were openly disputed. Anthropic cited an Opus 4.8 SWE-bench Pro improvement from 64.3 to 69.2, but antirez argued that including GPT 5.5 exposed how benchmarks can conflict with experienced quality, while others called for independent, uncontaminated evaluations or preferred benchmarks reflecting real software engineering. Steipete said GPT 5.5 had displaced Opus in OpenClaw internal tests and that Codex found more review issues, whereas another observation suggested Claude Code may suit zero-to-one work and Codex project maturation. The archive also records practical caveats: Codex context warnings when skills consume space, intermittent backend and regional transport failures, and a reminder that agents may find missing indexes or weak concurrency control but cannot make a moderately complex production system reliable merely by receiving an ambitious /goal prompt.

Local inference work focused on integration and measured tradeoffs. DwarfStar was described as a product spanning server, agent, CLI and tool calling rather than a rival inference engine to llama.cpp or MLX; removing the network boundary lets ds4-agent keep long tool-heavy chats cached and switch sessions immediately. Antirez implemented fast MiMo 2.5 inference and tool calling but said hand-written, GPT 5.5-judged tests favored DeepSeek v4 Flash every time, with DeepSeek producing better code, fixing bugs with fewer iterations, tokens and tool calls; MiMo 2.5 and MiniMax V2.7 therefore remained weaker candidates despite MiMo’s more generous quantization, though he acknowledged a possible hidden implementation bug and did not present the test as formal proof. DeepSeek v4’s KV-cache compression and indexed attention were praised, dense attention was called too computationally expensive near 100k local context, and Kimi 2.6 was said to be quantization-sensitive enough to require distributed inference. Elsewhere, a Qwen3-TTS MLX engine was being ported layer-by-layer to GGLM and C against Python+MLX and Rust+MLX-C oracles, highlighting both cross-platform ambitions and the hardware cost, coil whine and correctness burden of local work; skepticism also remained about sending computer-use data through a cloud agent merely to replace a few manual clicks.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.
Discussion centered on MCP, narrow tool contracts, and machine-readable interfaces for agents.

Fun fact: we built 𝚙𝚔𝚐¹ yeaaars ago in service of this vision. I didn't want customers to have to worry about Node.js over here, and the CLI package over there. We deprioritized it because Git and Web took off massively, and CLI usage was more sporadic.

Now the situation is inverted. Every day, I hear from customers discovering Vercel after OpenClaw, Claude Code, or Codex not only introduce, but also onboard users to our agentic infrastructure. Our CLI (as well as our MCP and SDKs) is a key enabler of this new wave.

¹ https://t.co/kidl1bmxjB

weeks.title: Claude exposes token costs while DwarfStar challenges MCP and benchmark claims
weeks.summary: Coding agents were discussed less as chatbots than as operating environments: Claude Code gained Opus 4.7 fast mode, token-attribution diagnostics and managed-agent controls, while Codex users described parallel sessions, autonomous issue triage and cloud-hosted execution. Alongside those workflow gains, builders argued over local inference architecture, model selection, MCP, context costs and whether benchmark progress reflects real-world coding ability.
details: Claude Code’s concrete changes centered on speed, observability and enterprise execution. Fast mode now defaults to Opus 4.7 via /fast; the forthcoming /usage command attributes tokens, including downstream usage, to Skills, Agents, MCPs and Plugins; and Claude Console now shows which prompt segment changed on a cache miss and its token cost. Claude Managed Agents added self-hosted sandboxes, MCP tunnels into protected services, live swapping of tools, MCP servers and vault IDs, and automatic offloading of MCP outputs above 100k tokens to sandbox files. Boris Cherny’s workflow advice was to use auto mode to eliminate permission prompts and run several sessions in parallel; he also said Opus 4.7 usually makes Plan Mode unnecessary, though compacting before returning to planning may prevent confusion.

Codex users described increasingly autonomous but still inspectable workflows. Peter Steinberger split knowledge work, learning and reading into the Codex Mac app while using cmux plus Codex CLI for coding; he built an autotriage skill that reads VISION.md and only autonomously tackles issues or PRs that fit the project, are inferable from code with high confidence, have a clear fix and can be live-tested, using a VM and computer vision to verify changes before his manual review. For large refactors he recommended requiring a scratch log of decisions, tradeoffs and review fixes. He also put Codex in Cloudflare Firecracker boxes, delegated larger-project tests to crabbox and rendered Ghostty through WebAssembly, while others favored AGENTS.md iteration, visible modification output and direct observation for steering rather than treating sandboxing as sufficient assurance.

The week also exposed operational costs and interface disagreements. OpenAI said a Codex optimization hurt cache-hit rates during compaction in long-running sessions, drained limits faster, was rolled back and prompted account-limit resets; the same team disclosed that some production traffic uses the Pi harness and OpenCode, floated batch compute as a /slow mode, and claimed 99.98% uptime. Antirez opposed MCP and argued that a local agent controlling inference can detect malformed tool parameters and abort before wasting a long generation, directly manipulate logits and expose prefill progress; he preferred first building the best integrated agent and only later splitting it across a session-token protocol. By contrast, Claude expanded MCP support and tunnels, while practical debugging advice included checking extensions and AGENTS.md for context pollution and updating around suspected Node 26 undici problems when Copilot or Codex login failed.

Local-model builders challenged headline evaluations. Antirez released the alpha ds4-agent inside DwarfStar and credited its low latency to inference living inside the agent; after testing MiniMax M2.7 he rejected it for DwarfStar because of its license, limited context, steep slowdown as context grows and no real-world advantage over DeepSeek v4 Flash. He argued DS4F’s compressed/indexed attention remains usable at long contexts where vanilla attention does not, reported an F16/NAX path exceeding 700 tokens per second peak prefill on small contexts during QA, and found even old two-bit quants resilient in incomplete evals. Both he and badlogicgames said benchmarks can overstate practical gains: Qwen 3.6 27B looked strong for its size yet belonged below DS4F in real use, while badlogicgames saw shell-computer-use improvements but regressions across recent releases and suggested coding models may be nearing an S-curve because synthetic agent loops reduce human training signal and design or systems thinking is hard to capture through reinforcement learning.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Discussion centered on MCP, narrow tool contracts, and machine-readable interfaces for agents.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.

weeks.title: Claude adds persistent goal loops while Codex automates cloud review fleets
weeks.summary: Claude Code introduced /goal as a built-in Ralph loop that checks a stated completion condition against the transcript and keeps working, while /loop repeats iterative refactors and backlog work; Claude also launched Opus 4.7 fast mode and advised pre-warming prompt caches to reduce first-token latency. Codex users simultaneously demonstrated aggressive automation—continuous PR, issue, security, benchmark, and meeting-driven agents—but debated reliability, review discipline, token cost, and whether GPT-5.5’s temporary degradation undermined those workflows.
details: OpenClaw’s workflow was described as roughly 100 cloud Codex instances reviewing every PR and issue, finding old issues fixed by later commits, deduplicating reports, scanning commits for security problems, reproducing setups in ephemeral machines, recording before/after videos, and even opening PRs from meeting discussions. The author stressed conservative guardrails and no auto-merging, while building a skill that repeatedly invokes Codex /review until it finds no more defects; he warned that this still cannot repair bad system architecture, so a human ‘brain’ must remain the master model.

Computer use moved from demos into practical workflows: Codex used Peekaboo to open Telegram, talk to BotFather, and obtain a debugging token, and separately clicked through Google Cloud Admin to enable a missing API. Claude Cowork, guided by stored flight preferences, reportedly booked eight flights and five hotels while its user coded; Codex’s in-app browser added viewport choices, screenshot viewing, improved annotations, and more token-efficient browsing.

Claude’s usage guidance made the cost/intelligence tradeoff explicit: /usage now identifies token-heavy plugins, skills, patterns, and parallel agents; users were told to clear stale long sessions, prefer Sonnet or medium-effort Opus, and optionally disable subagents, accepting reduced intelligence. Claude separated forthcoming programmatic credits for Agent SDK, claude -p, GitHub Actions, and third-party SDK apps from interactive subscription limits, while Codex acknowledged incorrect limits and a roughly 48-hour GPT-5.5 capability degradation, fixed two suspected causes, reset limits, and encouraged /fast use.

Local-model discussion centered on DeepSeek V4 Flash Q2: antirez said two-bit quantization showed no observed tool-calling degradation and could run a quasi-frontier model on 128GB, but cautioned that PRO at two bits might be worse than Flash and too slow on a costly 512GB Mac Studio. He argued evals are essential despite being tedious, added benchmark-like prompts to imatrix calibration, and noted that standardized benchmarks invite optimization yet still correctly signal GPT-5.5’s general advantage over Opus; others began calibrating a Q2 quant from Pi coding sessions while admitting evaluation remained unresolved.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
The emphasis was on real-world evaluation, executable evidence, and deterministic guardrails.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.

People freaking out over my AI spend. What nobody sees: Part of what excites me so much about working on OpenClaw is that I'm trying to answer the question:

How would we build software in the future if tokens don't matter?

We constant run ~100 codex in the cloud, reviewing every PR, every issue. If a fix on main lands, @clawsweeper will eventually find that 6 month old issue and close it with an exact reference.

We run codex on every commit to review for security issues (as it's far too easy to miss).

We run codex to de-duplicate issues and find clusters and send reports for the most pressing issues.

We have agents that can recreate complex setups, spin up ephemeral https://t.co/Q1NRXLemEy machines, log into e.g. Telegram, make a video and post before/after fix on the PR.

There's codex that watch new issues and - if it fits our documented vision well, automatically create a PR of it. (that then another codex reviews)

We have codex running that scans comments for spam and blocks people.

We have codex instances running that verify performance benchmarks and report regressions into Discord.

We have agents that listen on our meetings and proactively start work, e.g. create PRs when we discuss new features while we discuss them.

We build https://t.co/bmA1XnoB7P to split all our projects into functional units to review and find bugs and regresssions.

We do the same split for security with Vercel's deepsec and Codex Security to find regressions and vulnerabilities.

All that automation allows us to run this project extremely lean.

sources.author: dwarkesh_sp
sources.text:
# The mistake of conflating intelligence and power

I had an interesting discussion recently. Someone asked me, what is intelligence? I said, the ability to achieve your goals across a wide range of domains. Okay, he says, then by that definition isn’t Donald Trump the intelligent person in the world, followed in quick succession by Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin?

To be clear, these people are obviously very competent and clever. But when you think of ASI, you don’t think of Trump, but more so. 

The person who kept pressing this question was correctly pointing out that I basically defined intelligence as power. And by this definition, Stalin was the most intelligent person who ever lived.

Now, of course, you could change the definition of intelligence to something more like, manipulate abstract concepts and rotate shapes. 

But notice that the most powerful people in the world do not max out this quantity. The correlation between extreme power and this kind of intelligence might be even weaker than the correlation between extreme power and height. The physicists are not running the world.

We tend to conflate power-seeking AI and superintelligent (in science and tech) AI. I’m not denying that AI can be power-seeking. Whatever skills and drives Donald Trump has could be embodied in a digital mind. I’m simply pointing out that the way AI systems are currently becoming smarter (by getting trained to be to be really good at specific economically valuable tasks like coding) is not that strongly correlated with power.

We often talk about power in this way that misunderstands how it is actually derived in our world. Our intuitions are primed by games like Diplomacy or Go, which are designed to isolate and reward a g loaded kind of strategic reasoning. 

But in the real world, power is more the product of having the authority and trust to get lots of people to collaborate with you, rather than some galaxy brain scheming capability. Trump is not powerful because his brain, considered in isolation, is the most effective optimization engine on Earth. He is powerful because the government which hundreds of millions of people consider legitimate gives him a lot of authority.

A group versus individual level analysis is useful here. As @GarettJones has written a lot about, individual IQ is only modestly correlated with individual income, but national IQ is strongly correlated with national outcomes. This is because intelligence has a lot of spillover effects - smarter societies cooperate more, save more, and can coordinate to build things like space shuttles and semiconductors. 

Richard Trevithick, who invented the high-pressure steam engine, died in poverty, buried in an unmarked pauper’s grave. But the fact that 18th and 19th century Britain had lots and lots of people like Trevithick contributed to Britain being able to set up a global empire and outcompete lots of backwards principalities around the world.

It seems to me that the right mental model is that automated firms will outcompete everyone else in normal capitalist ways, rather than a single AI outthinking everyone else.

weeks.title: GPT-5.5 context regressions overshadow Managed Agents and parallel security automation
weeks.summary: Builders paired GPT-5.5/Codex with /goal, skills, parallel ephemeral sandboxes, and automated evidence capture, but several practitioners reported that GPT-5.5 stopped reading context reliably and sometimes reversed work after being questioned, prompting a return to gpt-5.3-codex. Claude shipped Managed Agents with multi-agent orchestration and rubric-driven improvement plus extensive Claude Code reliability fixes, while debates focused on where agent instructions, tests, linting, and human design actually provide trustworthy guardrails.
details: Concrete releases included Peekaboo 3.0 for action-first macOS computer use with unified screenshots/UI detection and cleaner CLI/MCP JSON, Crabbox-based bug reproduction and Windows terminal E2E testing, and Vercel’s open-source deepsec orchestrator for parallel security reviews in cloud sandboxes. OpenClaw automation recreated exact bugs in disposable environments, ran ten sessions in parallel, verified fixes, and generated before/after screen recordings—including real Telegram login—while Codex was also used to build Sonos, WhatsApp, X, GitHub, Discord, Spotify, iMessage, MCP-to-CLI, ElevenLabs voice, and second-opinion integrations.

Claude Managed Agents delegated work to specialized subagents with separate context windows but a shared container and filesystem, adding an outcomes loop, ‘dreaming’ for self-learning, and webhooks. Claude Code’s fixes addressed more than 10MB of piped stdin, clean resume after Mac sleep, runaway memory from malformed stdio MCP output, prompt caching for subagent summaries, full use of 1M-token windows, resilient parallel shell calls, MCP tool-list retries, and preservation of images in structured tool results.

The strongest workflow advice was to design foundations semi-manually—human architecture, mixed hand-and-agent implementation—then delegate lower-risk code rather than assuming a model is uniformly trustworthy. Tests can constrain an agent but create false confidence when the agent also writes them; AGENTS.md can be ignored, and lint enforcement has no silver bullet because reminders may be ignored, automatic linting may force unwanted turns, and pre-commit hooks only run when the model commits. For nontechnical collaboration, HTML with auto-refresh was recommended as an immediate visual feedback surface, whereas engineering review was said to work better through code plus annotation tools, reserving Markdown for context priming such as AGENTS.md and prompt templates.

Local inference claims were similarly qualified: DeepSeek V4 Flash was called the standout quasi-frontier local model that fits 128GB at usable speed, yet even M3 Ultra/M5 Max hardware was described as barely fast enough for serious work. On-disk KV caching reduced prefill pressure to roughly 400 tokens per second, leaving generation latency as the bottleneck; q2 and q4 were said to run at similar speed because routed experts consume little inference time and Q2 dequantization is not free. The suggested local-agent UI exposes streamed tools, prefill progress, and model reasoning instead of hiding long generations.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.

- system reminders injected by harness to tell model "please run linter". can inject after agent turn if files where modified. relies on model to do the thing. model might ignore system reminder.
- no system reminder, run automatically if agent turn modified files. needs to trigger a turn if linter reports errors/warnings. not what you want all the time.
- precommit hook. got that by default everywhere. but that requires the model to commit. also not what you want all the time.

so "easy to write a lint for" is true. kinda. there's no silver bullet.

lots to unpack, i'll try my best!

> specify all the essential code
i found the greatest success creating the foundations semi-manually (design by brain, implementation by hand + agent), then playing with that for a while to shake out any inconsistencies. not much different to working pre-agent, except the agent can help me speed up that phase. a good foundation can then somewhat coerce the model into generating non-horrible code often (but not always).

> leave gaps that are ok for LLMs fill in (knowing their shortcomings)?

the biggest issue is that we have no clear way of determining what the model can be trusted with and what it can not be trusted with. the same model, on the same task can output entirely different code just because of a single word difference in the input.

but as you identified, it's not all or nothing. not all code is equally important, or needs to be perfect. plenty of oportunity to use an untrustworthy code generator for these parts without looking much.

also, as you pointed out, you can further constraint the agent by tests/verification, tho that can also give you a false sense of guardrails, especially when you let the agent generate those for you without looking.

> a more compressed version of the source code that is higher signal to read (written in English, describes the intent directly, you don’t need to read lots of code to see the intent/ideas of the author)

so, first of all, our dear old friend shannon has a few words to say about compression, loss, and signals. but i'll skip that :)

the problem with intent is that it's not enough to arrive at a functioning system imo. think about the back and forths between pms/designers (intent) and engineering teams. ask yourself why we need those back and forths and what it means for intent + agent pair ups. i'm not sure this can be solved.

what your clanker analyzed was the intro of truncation info in the read and other tools. what your clanker can not analyze is additional context expressed in context files and extensions i'm using. hence, your clankers analysis is incomplete by construction.

Below is a clanker analysis of builder, which doesn't have a read tool at all, and just spits out total line counts for bash/powershell calls. that is much less than what e.g. the read tool in pi supplies as contextual information. so, if builder is your baseline on how to do this, i'd think pi does OK, as it outputs more info than builder.

this can or can not work, depending on what's already in  context, what model you are using, etc. in gpt 5.5 it seems like it is now working worse, while other models have no problem following the simple rule set.

weeks.title: Codex extends autonomous goals as DeepSeek v4 Flash runs locally
weeks.summary: Codex users described a shift from short coding assists toward long-running, self-checking work: /goal improved instructions, Auto-Review cut approval prompts, and teams wired review-and-fix agents into every commit. In parallel, local-model builders pushed DeepSeek v4 Flash selective 2-bit quantization and debated prompt-cache discipline, tool schemas, and whether dependence on subsidized hosted agents would last.
details: OpenAI’s Codex team said small tweaks let GPT-5.5 work for days on tasks such as building an OS kernel, finding critical bugs, and optimizing database schemas, while calling /goal potentially consequential because good instructions matter more for extended runs. Auto-Review became the internal default and was claimed to reduce approvals by roughly 200×; a playful persistent pet carried context while multitasking, and Codex was explicitly pitched to non-coders as browser-capable general computer work.

Concrete automation moved from demos into repository operations. Steipete ran Codex on every main-branch commit to find regressions or security issues, spawn a fixing PR, review that fix, and repeat for up to five loops; clawsweeper added Codex-style review and automerge, while Crabbox supplied ephemeral macOS, Linux, and Windows machines and Blacksmith supplied up to 32-vCPU test runners. Codex also worked around GitHub rate limits through the browser and created a suitably permissioned Cloudflare API key, illustrating both useful autonomy and the need for sandboxing and permission controls.

Claude Code focused on operational polish: push notifications when long jobs finish or need input, more than 50 CLI stability/performance fixes, lower Linux memory use, faster resume and startup, stable auth, and concurrent MCP-server connections. Its built-in Claude Platform skill could migrate model names, prompts, and effort settings to Opus 4.7, configure Managed Agents, and apply prompt caching; hackathon projects combined orchestration, persistent memory, MCP tools, sandboxed Python, and constrained prompts, including MedKit’s citation allowlist and ARIA’s 17 MCP tools.

Local inference became a serious engineering alternative rather than a small-model novelty. Antirez reported DeepSeek v4 Flash working as a coding agent on an M3 Max with 128GB by quantizing routed experts to roughly 2-bit while retaining routing, shared experts, and projections at 8-bit; he cited 21 tokens/s, 130 tokens/s prefill, compact KV caches suitable for disk checkpoints, and working tool calls, while building a specialized Metal inference server. Others warned hosted Codex economics may change and advised diversifying providers, but also stressed lean system prompts and tool sets: changing tools mid-turn can destroy prompt-cache hits, whereas pi’s cached WebSocket delta mode claimed 66% more throughput by sending only new context.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.

sources.author: badlogicgames
sources.text:
i'm afraid that's not how tools and prompt caching work. tools are early in the context, basically:

- system prompt
- tools
- user & assistant messages & tool results

if you change tools, you only get a cache hit for the system prompt (and some tools), and none for anything after tools.

tools do become available next turn currently. i believe your definition of turn is different tho. a turn is triggered by a user prompt, then we process assistant messages + tool calls and tool execution until we get a final assistant message without tool calls. that's when the agent loop returns control to you. and that's where it's save to mess with tools (and other things).

that will still fuck up your prompt cache next turn.

sources.author: badlogicgames
sources.text:
the assumption is that one agent turn (composed of multiple steps, i.e. intermittent assistant messages with tool calls, tool execution, final assistant message) is run with a static context, which includes the system prompt, tools, and message history.

that context is snapshotted at the start of the agent turn, so people can't do dumb things and then send issues because they don't understand they did a dumb thing.

switching out tools mid agent turn is theoretically possible, if we don't snapshot them, along with the system prompt and messages. but it means you break the prompt cache.

happy to not snapshot the tools and for you to reap what you sow :D

sources.author: mitsuhiko
sources.text:
Tool definitions are a bit different because a transformer can attend to any earlier token in the context. In theory a tool schema inserted later is visible, but model has been trained on a protocol where tools are declared in trusted setup before the assistant turn, then the user asks, then the model emits a special tool-call form.

Placement matters because role/order/format are part of the learned signal for "this is a real executable capability" not just text. Late markers can be read, but they are unexpected and may look like user content or prompt injection.

The whole setup is super crude in a way and I'm afraid that the current behavior will be with us for a while given hoe people train these things.

weeks.title: GPT-5.5 broadens Codex while Claude blames harnesses for quality regressions
weeks.summary: The week paired GPT-5.5 and a much broader Codex app with a frank argument over whether recent agent quality problems came from models or harnesses. Builders also tested large-scale review orchestration and found DeepSeek v4 Flash unusually capable under aggressive local quantization, though hardware, speed, and subscription economics remained real constraints.
details: Codex introduced GPT-5.5 across paid plans alongside full browser use, global dictation, a non-developer mode, safer Auto-Review, in-app documentation/PDF viewing, Chronicle memory, and a new default image model for website starting points and game assets. Chronicle, initially a token-hungry Mac/Pro research preview, builds memories from day-to-day computer work; users enable Memories and then Chronicle in Personalization. The team also reported a brief partial outage, said Codex assisted remediation but a human supplied the decisive insight, and restored image generation afterward.

Anthropic’s post-mortem said the perceived Claude Code quality regression came from three Claude Code/Agent SDK harness issues, not regressed models or the Claude API; Cowork was affected because it uses that SDK. Fixes landed in 2.1.116+, with advice to update and use Opus 4.7 at xhigh/max effort, while the team promised user-matching dogfood configurations and evals that isolate system-prompt changes; separate Opus 4.7-in-Claude-Code reports were still under investigation. Claude Code also previewed /ultrareview, a cloud fleet of bug hunters for critical auth or migration changes, and rebuilt web components for speed and reliability.

Agent orchestration advice was specific and somewhat skeptical of breadth for its own sake. Poteto recommended best-of-N races, adversarial review, multiple independent reproductions, and model specialization on one or a few hard problems rather than juggling ten unrelated jobs; verification should include running the app, reproducing the fault, and proving the fix. Steipete’s clawsweeper put 50 Codex instances on issue/PR triage, while acpx 0.6.0 added Claude system-prompt controls, session pruning, embeddable turn handles, persistent-session and WSL path fixes, and hardened queues; another practitioner preferred minimal per-session scope and a tidy agents.md over long instruction dumps.

Antirez found DeepSeek v4 Flash’s selectively quantized GGUF the first local setup that felt near-frontier: about 86GB on a 128GB M3 Max, routed experts at q2 and the rest at q8, roughly 7.5 tokens/s initially, functioning tool calls, and successful handling of Claude Code’s approximately 25k-token prompt/tool preamble. He still placed it around year-old frontier quality, observed Metal doubled prompt processing without speeding generation, and found DeepSeek v4 Pro via Claude Code cost about $1 per hour of intense use versus bundled OpenAI subscription tokens. The debate was therefore not simply open versus closed: Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.6 were called inadequate as general coding agents, Kimi K2.6 was suggested for future-proof open-weight development, and broken streamed tool calls plus fallback paths that send entire prompts showed that harness details can dominate model comparisons.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.

sources.author: rauchg
sources.text:
Coding agents will be the foundation of all superintelligence. 

At a minimum, coding ability is indistinguishable from 'proficiency with computers'. Great coding agents like Claude Code master bash, filesystems, configuring and installing programs…

But it's also about self-improvement. A coding agent has the ability to examine its source, its state, its skills, its instructions… it can propose changes to itself (with human supervision and audit trail, I recommend), or even mutate itself directly.

In retrospect, this should be obvious. "What I cannot create, I cannot understand". Coding fluency has given models a deeper understanding of all computer and knowledge work. To master programs, you must be able to create them.

sources.author: poteto
sources.text:
i'm increasingly convinced that the value of orchestrating many agents in parallel comes from going deep, not broad. you want to go deeper on a single or a few problems, so you can maximize your chances of getting great results:

- best of N style races to find the best solution
- adversarial review 
- multiple agents trying to repro a reported issue
- use different models for different types of workloads

to quote @mattpocockuk, "code is not cheap". 

this beats trying to context switch across many agents working on 10 different problems. the bottleneck is still me trying to remember and keep in my own context window what my agents work on. i think there will be ways to solve this with better ui.

there's also the element of trust. the more trust you have, the higher up the perspective ladder you can go. when you have little trust, you must micromanage each and every agent. when you can let go, you can delegate more. this is exactly like managing people!

weeks.title: Codex expands beyond coding as Opus 4.7 breaks repository instructions
weeks.summary: Codex expanded from a terminal coding agent into a broader app with computer use, an in-app browser, image generation/editing, multi-terminal and SSH support, automations, rich-document editing, and more than 90 plugins, while Claude Code shipped Opus 4.7, auto-approved safe commands, usage diagnostics, and a native binary. The week’s sharpest debate was whether those agentic gains outweighed instruction-following, security, cache-cost, and permissions problems: builders praised longer autonomous runs but reported Opus 4.7 violating AGENTS.md and warned that stronger reverse-engineering models raise the cost of weak security practices.
details: OpenAI’s Codex team described Mac computer use as able to operate precisely in the background using more than screenshots, and said /compact was coming after user requests. They also reset rate limits for Codex’s anniversary and claimed GPT-5.4 /fast has a plausible path to an order-of-magnitude speedup this year, framing compute efficiency and hard engineering as Codex’s core advantages.

Anthropic put Opus 4.7 into Claude Code and characterized it as more precise, more agentic, better with ambiguity and long-running work, and able to carry context across sessions. Auto mode routes permission requests through a model classifier so safe commands can run without babysitting; a separate /fewer-permission-prompts skill mines session history for repeatedly approved Bash and MCP commands and proposes allowlist entries, while /usage explains costs from parallel sessions, subagents, cache misses, and long contexts.

Claims about Opus 4.7 met concrete pushback: badlogicgames showed it committing despite AGENTS.md prohibiting that, later citing AGENTS.md in a pull-request comment and retaining ‘tail anxiety,’ and concluded that a model unable to honor repository instructions was unusable compared with Opus 4.6, 4.5, and 4.1. Anthropic simultaneously made xhigh the default effort level—between high and max—and advised controlling 4.7’s higher token use with effort, task budgets, or brevity prompts.

Infrastructure and workflow builders moved toward custom agent factories rather than one generic assistant. Vercel open-sourced Open Agents atop Fluid, Workflow, Sandbox, and AI Gateway for organizations whose monorepos, institutional knowledge, and integrations exceed off-the-shelf agents; pi adopted auto-closing of unapproved issues and PRs because most incoming agent-written reports were low-signal, and OpenClaw emphasized sandboxing, allowlists, credential isolation, rapid hardening, and published advisories as necessary responses to increasingly capable reverse-engineering models.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Discussion centered on MCP, narrow tool contracts, and machine-readable interfaces for agents.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.

sources.author: bcherny
sources.text:
1/ Auto mode = no more permission prompts

Opus 4.7 loves doing complex, long-running tasks like deep research, refactoring code, building complex features, iterating until it hits a performance benchmark.

In the past, you either had to babysit the model while it did these sorts of long tasks, our use --dangerously-skip-permissions.

We recently rolled out auto mode as a safer alternative. In this mode, permission prompts are routed to a model-based classifier to decide whether the command is safe to run. If it's safe, it's auto-approved.

This means no more babysitting while the model runs. More than that, it means you can run more Claudes in parallel. Once a Claude is cooking, you can switch focus to the next Claude.

Auto mode is now available for Opus 4.7 for Max, Teams, and Enterprise users. Shift-tab to enter auto mode in the CLI, or choose it in the dropdown in Desktop or VSCode.

sources.author: bcherny
sources.text:
👋 1h prompt cache is nuanced actually. It costs more for cache writes, and less for cache reads. Whether you benefit from cheaper cache reads depends on your usage pattern -- context window size, whether the query is the main agent or subagent, etc.

We have been testing a number of heuristics to give subscribers better prompt cache hit rates, which means lower token usage and lower latency, when it works. But this effect is far from uniform due to the nuance above. Say you use 1h cache for an agent, but only used the agent to make a single query -- in this case the 1h cache would be wasted and you'd be overcharged.

At this point we have rolled out 1h prompt cache by default in a number of places for subscribers to optimize cache duration based on real usage patterns, but we actually keep it at 5m for many queries also (eg. subagents, which are rarely resumed so you'd be paying for them even though they do not benefit from 1h). We also are not defaulting API customers to 1h yet -- this needs more testing to make sure it's a net improvement on average.

Separately, when we do this kind of experimentation, we use experiment gates that are cached client-side. When you turn off telemetry we also disable experiment gates -- we do not call home when telemetry is off -- so Claude reads the default value, which is 5m. We will soon be changing the client side default to 1h for a few queries, since we now feel good that it is a small token savings on average for those queries. We will also give you env vars to force 1h and 5m.

In any case, the token savings is nowhere near 12x unfortunately. It is a small win though, that we have been in the process of rolling out to everyone. Hope the explanation helps.

More here: https://t.co/06IJFDFvye

People of pi. The great @steipete has graced our repository with a bespoke slop PR to fix cache affinity in the OpenAI Responses provider, which should lead to better prompt caching.

And the new "pi contribution model (tm)" is now live. Here's how it works:

- If you send a PR, it gets autoclosed, unless you've previously been approved by a maintainer.
- If you send an issue, it gets autoclosed, unless you've previously been approved by a maintainer.

All auto-closed issues are triaged daily. 

- Issues that follow CONTRIBUTING.md and are worthwhile will be reopened.
- Issues that are exceptionally well written get an "lgtmi" comment from me or @mitsuhiko, which will approve all your future issues automatically. No more auto-closing.
- Issues that are well written AND offer a PR get an "lgtm" comment from me or @mitsuhiko, which will approve all your future issues and PRs automatically. No more auto-closing.

I, the idiot who has to go through all the closed slop daily, mark the last issue I processed with the "last read" label. If your issue is below that and hasn't been opened, then it did not meet the quality standard. You may or may not receive a reply on why the issue was not opened, depending on my time and mood.

Accounts that:
- Let their agents slop a book into the issue tracker repeatedly
- Otherwise behave badly

will get their account blocked across all my repositories. no exceptions. not takesies backsies.

I get anywhere between 30-50 issues per day. Most of them are agent garbage. This is the only way to keep me sane and ensure the issue and PR trackers have actual good signal.

weeks.title: GPT-5.4 dominates reverse engineering while minimalist Pi workflows reject tool sprawl
weeks.summary: Practitioners compared frontier coding models in demanding work and strongly favored GPT-5.4/Codex for complex reverse engineering, while still treating human line-by-line review as essential for production changes. They also shipped concrete harness, observability, local-model, and trace-sharing tools, while debating whether MCP, web search, subagents, and extension-heavy setups improve work or merely add indirection and token waste.
details: Antirez ran long autonomous sessions of Claude Code Opus 4.6 and Codex GPT-5.4 at maximum thinking budget in refreshed cloned directories, and called the gap on serious reverse engineering ‘brutal’: GPT-5.4 could combine hardware knowledge with disassembly while Opus was borderline useless for that task. For a large Redis feature, however, he still reviewed every generated line and made many changes, reporting a huge speedup rather than autonomy; others summarized model choice as GPT-5.4 for the best well-rounded results at highest cost, GPT-5.4-Mini for cheap fast work with escalation on hard cases, and GPT-5.3-Codex when code generation is the only concern.

Claude Code’s rapid shipping exposed organizational tradeoffs as well as model capability. Boris Cherny said Claude had increased Anthropic engineering velocity by hundreds of percent but moved bottlenecks into review, regression prevention, CI, merge queues, source-control reliability, and feature communication; he recommended letting the model invoke plan mode, skills, and settings, generalizing rather than duplicating features, keeping incomplete ideas opt-in, and using the stable channel if latest moves too quickly. Claude Code v2.1.85 also made @-mentions three times faster in huge repositories by adding fileSuggestion so enterprises can replace its Rust/NAPI indexer with Sourcegraph or an internal code index.

Tool builders shipped practical interoperability work: OpenClaw added the efficient TurboQuant-based inferrs server alongside self-hosted models, LM Studio, and Ollama support; its experimental native Codex harness lets Codex own threads, resume, compaction, and app-server execution, trading some personality for stronger long-horizon persistence. CodexBar 0.20 added Perplexity and OpenCode Go, account switching without re-login, corrected duplicated Claude token/cost accounting, merged session and provider cost history, and tracked 16 providers; local-model advocates nevertheless conceded that local models lag frontier coding systems, recommending Qwen3-Coder-Next on a powerful Mac for speed and tool calling and smaller models for speech cleanup, embeddings, NER, and paraphrasing.

The clearest workflow advice was deliberately minimalist: start pi vanilla, add an extension only for recurring pain, put project-specific recurring instructions in AGENTS.md, and prefer cloning a dependency’s repository and reading raw code/docs over injecting noisy, stale web-search output into context. Badlogicgames said subagents were mainly useful for gathering disposable context or experiments and preferred pi’s observable /tree branches; he also built pi-share-hf to publish coding-agent sessions as Hugging Face datasets with three layers of PII defense, but stressed those defenses were not sufficient, agent-based detection could burn many tokens, OSS sessions were safer, and users must inspect both code and traces before publishing.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Open weights, private inference, quantization, and hybrid local/frontier setups gained attention.
Discussion centered on MCP, narrow tool contracts, and machine-readable interfaces for agents.

sources.author: bcherny
sources.text:
👋 Appreciate the feedback.

Since we introduced Claude Code at Anthropic, engineering velocity has increased hundreds of %, and the rate at which it is increasing is itself accelerating.

The velocity is very much not performative -- we're actively trying to figure out how to build effectively when all of the code is written by Claude. Claude has  accelerated the pace at which we ship, and as a result we've been hitting all sorts of new bottlenecks: code review and regression prevention, CI and merge queues, source control reliability, etc. We're working through each of these as they come up, and now have good answers for a number of them.

One of these bottlenecks is figuring out how to best communicate new features to our users. My pov is we need to be doing much better here. The problem isn't that we are releasing quickly, the problem is that we should design features in a way where you don't need to know about them to benefit from them. This is the case for much of what we build, and we need to make it the case for all of it.

To share how we think about it, there's a few ways to approach it from a product design pov:
- Make it so the model can do things for you (eg. enter plan mode, invoke skills, configure your settings)
- Generalize features rather than create new parallel features
- Make features opt-in until we do the above
- Have Claude monitor feature usage and brainstorm/build ways to improve usage while simplifying the system

We try to do all of the above, but as you said, it's not perfect yet, and this is something we're working through. If you prefer a lagging version, you can also use the Claude Code stable release (not latest). We're intentionally being open about what we're seeing, since our customers are seeing the same thing and at least part of our job is helping companies navigate this new way of doing engineering.

Re: source code leak -- it was unintentional, but was also human error. There was a subtle bug that missed several rounds of manual review. We're working on how we can better catch it automatically next time.

as more and more people start using pi, i now get this question often:

"what are essential extensions i should install?"

none. zero. start vanilla. only build/install something if you feel a recuring pain that you can't get rid of by reevaluating your workflow learned with another harness.

i have 2 extensions:
- promot-url-widget.ts in pi-mono/.pi/extensions: if a git issue/pr url is mentioned in a user message, it displays a little widget above the editor with the issue/pr title, submitter account id, and link to cmd+click. if i have multiple sessions open i know immediately what it's about
- pi-diff-viewer, simple slash command spawning a GUI that lets me annotate a diff or any file in the working directory. once done, annotations are feed back to pi as a prompt, with a request for the model to act on the annotations.

this is all i ever use. no, i don't use web search, mcp, multi-agents, whatever. i'm likely still outperforming you productivity wise with less token usage.

addendum:

"but how do you do without websearch?"

first, i'd like you to proxy your harness of choice and see what garbage their respective web search/fetch tool actually pushes into your agent's context. 

second, 99% of the time, the only reason you let your agent use web search is to fetch docs. these may be outdated or incomplete.

i stead, i let my agent clone the repo of the dependency, analyse its code (or docs if available in the repo in their raw, non-html-rendered form) and optionally let it spit out an .md file that summarizes what it needs to know for future use. less token waste, more precise, reusable and updatable.

"but my subagents"

knocm yourself out. for me, subagents are only useful to:

- gather context
- try out things and throw them away

in both cases i use pi's /tree instead. i have full observability, can take any learnings with me to a previous poibt in the session via summarization or writing a markdown file on disk.

bonus: all the branches i took stay in the same session file, should i ever need to revisit them (i usually don't, sessions are generally ephemereal for me)

weeks.title: Codex capacity resets collide with Claude caching and subscription disputes
weeks.summary: Codex and Claude Code users focused on scaling strain, subscription boundaries, prompt-cache efficiency, and practical differences between coding agents. They also debated plan mode, self-modifying harnesses, model quality, terminal UX, and whether progress in coding agents generalizes to less verifiable knowledge work.
details: OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux said unexpected Codex rate-limit pressure led him to reset usage limits for every plan, while banning fraudulent accounts recovered compute; he later floated off-peak incentives and peak-time surge multipliers to smooth demand. He argued that demand would temporarily outstrip AI supply and that capacity plus model efficiency would decide the winners, while noting that the Codex App had overtaken the VS Code extension and CLI and that business and enterprise customers could start with zero seats and pay as they go.

On Claude Code, Boris Cherny announced an experimental NO_FLICKER terminal renderer, enabled with CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1, that most internal users preferred despite acknowledged early tradeoffs and that added mouse events. Responding to power-user complaints, he said 1M context was free and could be effectively returned to 200k behavior with CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=20, denied that Opus 4.6 itself had changed, recommended /bug to diagnose regressions and /effort to trade tokens for intelligence, and attributed tighter limits and reliability problems to rapid growth rather than broken caching.

A dispute over third-party harnesses centered on economics and prompt caching. Cherny said Claude subscriptions were optimized for Claude's own workload, whereas API keys and overages remained appropriate for third-party tools, offered refunds, and submitted OpenClaw PRs to improve cache efficiency. Mario Zechner agreed that subscription restrictions made sense, argued that many harnesses unnecessarily bust provider caches, praised Anthropic's explicit caching API over opaque automatic caching, and advised custom-harness builders to study the OpenClaw fixes or use pay-as-you-go.

Planning advice diverged sharply. Peter Steinberger said he never uses Codex plan mode and prefers simply talking to the agent; Zechner instead described planning as an exploratory conversation that builds the developer's understanding, often without using the final artifact, and proposed discussing without edits, collaboratively refining a Markdown plan in an editor, then recording exactly which files a fresh session should read. He resisted harness-prescribed workflows because exploration may require throwaway code or APIs, not only read, ls, and grep.

The posts also tested broader claims about agent capability. Zechner argued coding is unusually tractable because training data is abundant and outputs are verifiable, predicted limits on moving from local changes to whole-system architecture, and said open weights and smaller models should catch up; he characterized OpenClaw and pi's notable idea as unrestricted self-modification, but warned that prompt injection's 'lethal trifecta' blocks safe mass deployment. Steinberger said OpenClaw was mostly built with Codex, preferred Codex as a software engineer while finding Claude/Opus more entertaining, and described an OpenClaw QA loop where an orchestrator creates synthetic tasks, verifies results, and launches a repair subagent on failure. Elsewhere, Antirez rejected Gemma 4's emphasis on ELO and said dense Qwen 3.5 27B remained stronger in its memory class, while Zechner reported that GPT-5.4's 1M context was already 40% consumed in his use and cautioned that newer models can regress in some areas.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.
Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.
Teams focused on persistent loops, orchestration, parallel agents, and bounded autonomy.

sources.author: bcherny
sources.text:
Thanks for the feedback.

> Scrollback gutted - session history is barely scrollable. I can't review my own conversation.

can you tell me more about this? how do I repro?

> Rate limits hit harder - prompt caching appears broken since March 23. Sessions that lasted hours now drain in 90 minutes.

prompt caching is working correctly, and we've been shipping optimizations to make it work better. we announced reduced rate limits at peak recently due to our infra being strained because of really fast user growth. we're working around the clock to make this better, and landing improvements every day. please bear with us as we scale up -- it's really hard growing at this scale and we are working as hard as we can to keep up and serve everyone.

> 1M context forced, no opt-out - extra usage required, 200k toggle removed. I didn't ask for this tradeoff.1M context

not quite -- 1m context is free, and does not require extra usage. you can opt out by setting CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=20 to go back to 200k context window

> Opus quality regression - execution bias overrides explicit instructions. The agent pushes into wrong directions constantly. Complex multi-step tasks that worked weeks ago now fail routinely.

we have not changed opus 4.6 since rolling it out. if there's a regression, it's either in claude code, or due to a new memory or CLAUDE.md that your claude is pulling in. to debug, can you run /bug the next time you see this and post the feedback id here?

> Every recent update optimizes for mass adoption. That's great - but the features power users already built themselves now come at the cost of the reliability we depend on.  I'm not asking for special treatment. I'm asking: don't make your highest-paying subscribers collateral damage of growth.  The tools I've built on Claude Code are my business. When the foundation shifts weekly, that's not iteration - it's instability.

i totally hear you. we want to support both power users and everyone else. recent reliability issues have been a result of completely insane user growth. working as hard  as we can to scale up all our services. 

next time you hit specific issues, feel free to tag me directly.
