sources.author: badlogicgames
sources.text:
recommended viewing. lots of things i don't agree with, insightful regardless. wall of text incoming.

"we know, if it works in coding, it works everywhere, coding is the hard thing"

quite the oposite. coding, or program generation is comparatively easy. you have great signals, great existing training data, that even encode most of the workflows of an entire industry. and outputs are more or less pretty verifiable and self-contained. especially compared to other knowledge work, where outputs are usually not machine verifiable in the same way, and are inputs to other systems, and more importantly, humansz that you can't model as easily.

there's a reason all labs jumped on coding immediately after one proofed it out.

and now they try to solve everything else by translating it into a coding task. this works for a lot of things, and can help with subtasks for all those other knowledge work tasks that are not verifiable or for which good training data acquisition is impossible/hard.

but that also means this approach has a natural cap.

"linus said ai now codes better than him"

that's lacking all the nuance. linus said that in the context of vibe coded hobby project of his, specifically about frontend/python code, both areas he has almost no experience in.

if you want to hear his full take, see 

https://t.co/Bw5WcM2nBV

minute 15. listen to it in full.

"... scaling laws, autoresearch, ..."

labs have gobbled up enormous amounts of additional, coding harness specific training data over the past 12 months, through Claude Code or Codex, and i'd attribute the jumps we've seen in model performance during the same timeframe to that. i personally lived through more than CC/Codex in terms of ai assisted coding, so my frame of reference may be a bit broader. but i personally did not experience e.g. opus 4.6 or Coded 5.4 to be huge jumps, in fact, in some areas they regressed compared to predecessor models.

my guess is that we are nearing saturation here, without a clear path away from "make these local changes" to "architect this entire system like a team of 10x super pros". i think that's largely due to the fact that the former is easy to encode in training data, while the later is not.

whenever that changes, we'll see a new noticable jump. i don't think we'll see it anytime soon. i do think we'll see open weights and smaller lab models catching up (and i'd love to help here). because the models we have are already immensely useful in our industry, despite being very imperfect tools. commoditization is necessary to prevent oligopolization and true competition, i think.

"openclaw and pi, two european projects"

finally, there's a section on openclaw (and pi) around minute 33. finally something i actually have 1st hand insights :)

first, apparently openclaw and pi being "two european" projects is unfathomal to andreesseen. which is extremely funny, as most of the best and most impactful folks in ai working on the core ML tech are not US citizens. him then asking "but wait, wasn't peter in the US when he build openclaw" is hilarious. what i can say on my end: any offers i got had a clause that had me stay where i am. i also have not submitted a 83(b). you can guess what that means :)

the only reason people leave for the US is the  money. the community and network aspects have greatly diminished over the past 15 years, especially after "let's all be remote" COVID times. it has always been bizarre to me as a kid who basically grew up with the internet, that physical location should mean anything in the 21st century. i can tell you that nothing about the current state of the US is enticing to many of my highly talented and capable non-US peers.

US companies will happily take in folks who enjoyed e.g. european social and education systems, to build their great scientific and techboligical breakthroughs. nothing wrong with that. egg on europes face for not being able to keep the talent around.

but american exceptionalism in tech will end as soon as money flows as easily in other regions. and that is much more likely after the recent polticial turmoil (tho i'm sure we in europe will invent new elegant ways to fuck this chance up).

"pi, the unix philosophie"

llm + shell + markdown + cron is not the breakthrough. that's basically what aider/claude code/etc invented, minus the cron jobs/hooks.

what openclaw and pi introduced was the concept of a self-modifying harness. an agent that can modify it's own capabilities. i don't think that's a huge breakthrough, possibly because my punny european mind doesn't allow me to see it as that, standing on the shoulders of giants, etc. others have done the same, before openclaw and pi. it's just that those precursors have severly limited the things the LLM can do due to very good security reasons.

openclaw initially did away with that, under the assumption that its users would be technical. pi never had safe guards because it's an expert tool. that openclaw escaped into normie space was unpredictable. and peter still suffers the consequences, toiling away on security work.

so yes, the unrestricted self-modifiability of openclaw and pi did show us a glimpse of the future of what agents can do.

but the real breakthrough will be the one, where we can have capable, self-modifiable agents like openclaw or pi + a solution to the lethal trifecta. and it appears that there are fundamental theoretical reasons, why a solution to the trifecta may be impossible.

that has implications for where and how such agents can be deployed for the near and mid term future. my mom will not have a claw for a while.

but i can also take a compliment and agree, that pi's composition is pretty sweet :)

"the agent has full introspection and can rewrite its own files"

yeah, turns out introspection is pretty important, and anti-introspection is anti-growth and improvement.

weeks.title: Codex wins developer praise for faster bug fixes and reliable skills
weeks.summary: One developer said Codex was markedly faster and better for bug fixes. They also found it more consistent and reliable at invoking skills.
details: Poteto's post was a direct comparative endorsement of Codex for a concrete coding workflow: fixing bugs. The claimed advantages were speed, bug-fix quality, and dependable skill invocation; the post did not provide a benchmark, competing model name, or detailed reproduction.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.

sources.author: poteto
sources.text: codex is just so much faster and better at bugfixes. also noticed it's much more consistent/reliable at invoking skills

weeks.title: Codex turns fixture configuration request into an unwanted library-wide refactor
weeks.summary: A request for a one-line Codex configuration change expanded into an unwanted library-wide refactor. The post illustrates how an agent can mistake a fixture-specific instruction for a request to change the product default.
details: Poteto asked Codex to configure a fixture app differently through a one-line config-file edit. Instead, Codex refactored the entire library so that the requested fixture behavior became the default, a concrete example of excessive scope and the need to state whether a change is local or global.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.

sources.author: poteto
sources.text: told codex to configure my fixture app differently (one line config file change) and it proceeds to refactor my entire library to make that the default

weeks.title: Claude manages while Codex codes in a two-agent division of labor
weeks.summary: One developer split the agent workflow into complementary roles: Claude as the manager and Codex as the coder. The post offered that concise division of labor without further evidence or implementation detail.
details: Poteto described Claude as 'the perfect manager' and Codex as 'the perfect coder.' The literal recommendation is a two-agent role distinction—Claude for direction or coordination, Codex for implementation—rather than a claim that either tool is best at every part of software work.
takeaways: Repository instructions, planning, reusable skills, and coding-agent practice drove the conversation.

weeks.title: Apple hardware inspires qualified case for AI-made quality at scale
weeks.summary: A developer partly agreed with concerns about AI-made quality, but argued that Apple's mass-produced hardware shows scale and quality are not inherently incompatible. They suggested guidance, scaffolding, and context engineering could eventually let AI tools produce quality at scale, while explicitly saying current systems are not there yet.
details: Poteto's reply held two positions at once: emphatic sympathy with the criticism being answered, and optimism that AI-assisted production need not sacrifice quality. Apple served as the counterexample because it mass-produces hardware products while maintaining a reputation for quality.

The proposed route was not unguided generation but carefully designed guidance, scaffolding, and context engineering around AI tools. The conclusion was deliberately provisional: quality at scale remains unrealized, yet the author argued builders should continue trying rather than treat today's limitations as permanent.
takeaways: Builders examined caching, compaction, retrieval, and durable memory across long-running sessions.

sources.author: poteto
sources.text: there's a big part of me that emphatically agrees, but also another that knows that Apple mass produces its hardware products. i think AI tools, with the right guidance and scaffolding/context engineering, could help us produce quality at scale. we're not there yet, but we should keep trying!
